lead: A buck converter can only step down and a boost can only step up. A buck-boost converter gets both from one inductor: the switch charges it from the source, then the switch opens and the inductor pushes that energy into the output. The output comes out inverted, and the same circuit works below or above the input voltage. The Cuk converter reaches the same gain with a capacitor carrying the energy in the middle, so the currents at both ports stay smooth. Both appear in battery equipment, LED drivers and negative-rail supplies.
prereq: You need: the on/off state method and volt-second balance from Buck converter and Boost converter.

sections.h3: The buck-boost circuit and its two states

blocks.text: Four parts sit around node A. The source V<sub>s</sub> (volts) feeds switch S, which connects it to node A. Inductor L (henries) runs from node A to the return rail. Diode D runs from the output node to node A, with its cathode at A. Capacitor C and load R sit between the output node and the return rail. This diode orientation makes the output negative.

Switch ON, for D·T seconds of each period T = 1/f. Here D is the duty ratio (0 ≤ D ≤ 1), T is the switching period in seconds and f = 1/T is the switching frequency in hertz. With the switch on, node A sits at V<sub>s</sub>, the diode cathode is the highest voltage in the circuit, so the diode blocks. The inductor sees v<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>s</sub> and its current rises in a straight line. The capacitor alone feeds the load.

Switch OFF, for the rest of the period. The inductor current cannot stop. It keeps flowing the same way as before, from node A down through L to the return rail, so node A falls until the diode conducts and supplies that current from the output node. The diode then holds node A at V<sub>o</sub>, which is negative, so v<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>o</sub> and the inductor current falls. The load current now comes from the return rail through R into the output node, then through the diode and the inductor, so the stored energy reaches the load.
V<sub>s</sub> is the input voltage in volts; V<sub>o</sub> is the output voltage in volts, negative with respect to the return rail; D is the duty ratio; T is the period in seconds.

The magnitude ratio |V<sub>o</sub>|/V<sub>s</sub> = D/(1 − D) equals 1 at D = 0.5. Below 0.5 the converter steps down, above 0.5 it steps up. Both jobs from one inductor give it the name step-down/step-up converter, or inverting regulator.

sections.h3: Stress, currents and what it costs

blocks.text: Blocking voltage. With the switch off, its two terminals sit at V<sub>s</sub> and V<sub>o</sub>, so it must block V<sub>s</sub> + |V<sub>o</sub>| = V<sub>s</sub>/(1 − D). The diode blocks the same. At 12 V input and D = 0.6 that is 30 V, not 12 V, and a 25 V MOSFET would fail.

Inductor current. The diode carries the load current only during the off-time, so the inductor average is I<sub>L</sub> = I<sub>o</sub>/(1 − D). The ripple is ΔI<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>·D/(L·f). Continuous conduction needs I<sub>L</sub> ≥ ΔI<sub>L</sub>/2, which gives L ≥ (1 − D)²·R/(2f).

Pulsed input current. The source supplies current only while the switch is on: a rectangle of height I<sub>L</sub> and width D·T. Its average is I<sub>s</sub> = D·I<sub>L</sub> = |V<sub>o</sub>|·I<sub>o</sub>/V<sub>s</sub>, which is just power balance. A practical buck-boost always has an input capacitor across the source. This capacitor absorbs the difference between the pulsed switch current and the smooth source current, so it carries a large ripple current and needs a low ESR.

Rough output. The diode feeds the output in pulses too, so the output capacitor also carries a large ripple current. That is the practical weakness of the buck-boost: two noisy ports, one small inductor.

Cuk (say "chook") rearranges the same parts. Inductor L1 runs from V<sub>s</sub> to node A, switch S from A to the return rail, capacitor C1 from A to node B, inductor L2 from B to the output node, diode D from B to the return rail with its anode at B and its cathode at the return rail, and C2 across the load. The output is inverted again.

ON: node A is at zero, so B sits at −V<sub>C1</sub> and the diode blocks. C1 discharges through the switch, driving the current of L2 and the load, while L1 charges from V<sub>s</sub>. OFF: the diode conducts and clamps B near zero, one diode drop above the return rail (B swings between −V<sub>C1</sub> and 0). The current of L1 flows through C1 into B and charges C1; at B it meets the current of L2 coming back from the load, and both return through the diode to the rail.
D·Vs + (1 − D)(Vs − VC1) = 0 → VC1 = Vs/(1 − D) = Vs + |Vo|

V<sub>C1</sub> is the average voltage across the coupling capacitor in volts; the other symbols are as before. Balancing L2 the same way gives V<sub>o</sub> = −V<sub>s</sub>·D/(1 − D), the buck-boost gain.

The gain is identical, the currents are not. L1 carries the source current and L2 the load current, both continuous, so ripple at each port is small and filtering is easy. The price is two inductors, plus C1 carrying the full input current as a large alternating current, so it is a film or ceramic part, not a small electrolytic.
SEPIC and Zeta move the same parts to get a positive output. The flyback in Isolated converters: flyback and forward is a buck-boost whose inductor is split into two coupled windings.

figure.caption: The worked example: 12 V in, D = 0.6, −18 V out. With the switch on, the source charges L; with it off, L drives its current up through the load and the diode, so the output node is pulled below the return rail. The Cuk does the same job with C1 at 30 V.

spec.aria: Top: the buck-boost circuit drawn twice. On: shaded loop from the 12 volt source through the closed switch and the inductor. Off: shaded loop from the inductor through the diode and the 10 ohm load, output minus 18 volts. Bottom: the Cuk circuit with L1, switch, coupling capacitor C1 at 30 volts, diode, L2, C2 and the load at minus 18 volts.

examples.question: A buck-boost converter takes 12 V from a battery and must deliver 18 V into a 10 Ω load. The switching frequency is 100 kHz and the inductor current is continuous. Find (a) the duty ratio, (b) the output current, (c) the average inductor current, (d) the voltage the switch must block, (e) the average source current, (f) the smallest inductance for continuous current. State the output polarity.
steps: Inductor average: I<sub>L</sub> = I<sub>o</sub>/(1 − D) = 1.8/0.4 = 4.5 A.
Switch stress: V<sub>s</sub> + |V<sub>o</sub>| = 12 + 18 = 30 V = V<sub>s</sub>/(1 − D) = 12/0.4.
Source current: I<sub>s</sub> = D·I<sub>L</sub> = 0.6 × 4.5 = 2.7 A. Power check: 12 × 2.7 = 32.4 W in, 18 × 1.8 = 32.4 W out.
Polarity: the output is −18 V with respect to the return rail, so the load and output capacitor connect in that sense.
Minimum inductance for CCM: L ≥ (1 − D)²R/(2f) = 0.4² × 10/(2 × 100 kHz) = 8 µH.
examples.answer: D = 0.6, I<sub>o</sub> = 1.8 A, I<sub>L</sub> = 4.5 A, switch stress 30 V, source current 2.7 A, L at least 8 µH, and the output is −18 V.

D = Vo / (Vs + Vo)
Io = Vo / R
IL = Io / (1 - D)

traps: Gain magnitude is D/(1 − D), not (1 − D)/D. Both give 1 at D = 0.5, so the error hides until another duty ratio.
Sign: the output is −V<sub>s</sub>·D/(1 − D). Writing +18 V loses the polarity mark and needs the capacitor and feedback divider reversed.
Switch stress is V<sub>s</sub> + |V<sub>o</sub>| (30 V here), not V<sub>s</sub> and not |V<sub>o</sub>|.
Inductor current is I<sub>o</sub>/(1 − D), not I<sub>o</sub>/D. The diode hands load current to the output only during the off-time.
In the Cuk converter, V<sub>C1</sub> = V<sub>s</sub> + |V<sub>o</sub>| = V<sub>s</sub>/(1 − D); it is not |V<sub>o</sub>| alone, and it is the largest voltage in the circuit.

quiz.q: State the voltage gain of the buck-boost converter in continuous conduction, with the output sign.
quiz.a: V<sub>o</sub> = −V<sub>s</sub>·D/(1 − D). The output is inverted.

quiz.q: Explain why the buck-boost output is negative.
quiz.a: The inductor charges with node A at +V<sub>s</sub> and discharges with node A pulled below the return rail by the diode. The diode ties the output node to node A during discharge, so the output is negative. Volt-second balance forces the minus sign.

quiz.q: A buck-boost runs from V<sub>s</sub> = 24 V at D = 0.75. Find the output magnitude and the switch blocking voltage.
The same 24 V, D = 0.75 design is built as a Cuk converter. Find the average voltage across the coupling capacitor and the output.
quiz.a: V<sub>C1</sub> = 24/0.25 = 96 V. The output is −72 V, the same gain.

quiz.q: Why is the useful duty ratio of a buck-boost kept well below 1?
quiz.a: Switch and diode block V<sub>s</sub>/(1 − D), and the inductor current is I<sub>o</sub>/(1 − D). At D = 0.9 both are ten times their low-D values, so device rating and conduction loss limit D long before the ideal gain grows large.

quiz.q: Compare the output capacitor ripple current of a buck-boost and a Cuk supplying the same load.
quiz.a: The buck-boost capacitor gets a pulse of height I<sub>L</sub> − I<sub>o</sub> for (1 − D)T and −I<sub>o</sub> for the rest, so ripple is large. In the Cuk, L2 delivers nearly flat current to the load, so capacitor ripple is small.

beyond: Not for the exam. The inverting output is rarely wanted, so most designs use a four-switch buck-boost: two half-bridges around one inductor that rewire themselves into buck or boost mode and keep a positive output. That is the chip inside many USB-C power-delivery chargers and battery-backed rails. The Cuk survives where a quiet negative rail matters, such as audio and instrument supplies, and its coupled-inductor form gets very low ripple from one magnetic core. Search 'four-switch buck-boost', 'SEPIC versus Cuk' and 'coupled inductor Cuk' to go further.
